I've recently been playing Skyrim with 4000+ mods in a 600GB package and it has been an amazing experience that is somehow more stable than vanilla Skyrim.  This is "LoreRim", A fascinating modpack that it aims to remake almost every single aspect of Skyrim under an entirely new gameplay philosophy, turning Skyrim into a modern action game. A lot of you have asked me about it since my 8K bread post and while I have only about 10 hours in this modpack so far, I can tell you that the amount of things LoreRim changes about Skyrim is nothing short of unbelieveable.   The world of Skyrim is heavily changed, every city has far more detail. there are new buildings, new dungeons, new quests, new people and way more dialogue options with existing people. Even the roads themselves have been heavily redesigned to reflect each hold's asthetic, it is something you seriously need to play to understand. It still manages to feel like Skyrim but its a very different, way more dense Skyrim.  The first most obvious change you notice is the visuals. Obviously, at 600GB, you expect this mod pack to look insane and it does. I had to run this on the "Default" preset rather than the Ultra preset because it is one of the most demanding games you could possibly run, Skyrim was never built to look like this but LoreRim somehow makes it work. Every single texture looks amazing, every single person looks completely different, LoreRim keeps everything lore-friendly hence the name so don't expect super models in this modpack but there are amazing looking people. You probably have seen my 8K bread post earlier and the entire game has that quality, armor sets in particular look incredible. It really makes Skyrim look like a 2026 game while keeping the original intent of its aesthetic intact.   Gameplay in LoreRim is something I've honestly barely scratched the surface of, so far. The modpack is built around a foundational mod called "Requiem", which makes Skyrim's world unlevelled, meaning the world no longer is scaled to you throughout the game and you absolutely will get destroyed if you try going into combat without assessing things and preparing in advance. You start off extremely weak and can barely kill skeevers, and then slowly work your way up from there. XP is given by completing quests and fighting enemies, not by using skills themselves like in Vanilla Skyrim. This is a huge change that also heavily effected how I play Skyrim at its core, I prioritized doing basic tasks like deliveries, sticking to roads, helping out locals in towns without venturing out until I levelled up enough and had enough coin to get decent gear and start tackling actual combat.  Speaking of combat, it is entirely different. There is a stances system, lock-on, parrying, dodging, and completely different animations. I have been doing a stealth archer build (yeah i know lmao) and its somehow been the most fun I've had doing stealth in Skyrim maybe ever, because there is just so much more depth to each encounter and how I balance archery with the new enemy AI that takes cover or rushes bow users. There is a heavy focus on builds and replays are heavily incentivized to experiment with different builds and ideas, you cannot be a jack of all trades anymore.  Now the biggest issue with this modpack is that you do need quite a beefy PC, I have been playing this at 4K 40-60FPS on a 9070XT with a Ryzen 3600 and 16GB of DDR4 ram which is far from the ideal specs at this resolution but it works well enough for me that I can stick with it and enjoy the game. the 600GB storage requirement is insane, however you can delete the 250GB download folder once its finished installing, bringing it down to 350GB to keep on an M.2 SSD as recommended by the author. Because this is a heavily curated mod list with a ton of work put into it by the author for stability and patching, I have only experienced 1 crash so far, which is genuinely more stable than a base vanilla Skyrim for me.   I will have a lot more to say about this modpack as I continue playing it and I may even have some insights from the author himself soon in future posts so stay tuned! If you wanna download it, I highly recommend looking up a tutorial on YouTube. It is basically a one click download and install.

UPDATE ON THE FUTURE OF BOLTZ 📢  Over the past couple of months, AI-assisted attackers have been targeting Boltz with increasing frequency, intensity and sophistication. Several of these attacks succeeded, but because Boltz is non-custodial, user funds were never at risk. The entirety of the risk was ours, and as a result of the losses incurred, on August 3rd we made the difficult decision to suspend the service to prevent further damage.  While working on a plan to bring Boltz back over the past days, we had to accept one painful insight: as a bootstrapped five-person startup, we simply don't have the resources to withstand the current level of attacks in the long run.  Today, we are happy to announce that a group of veteran Bitcoiners came forward to help, bringing the capital and engineering power the project needs. They have agreed to take over Boltz and continue the service. Work to find and fix the vulnerabilities is already under way, with the goal of bringing swaps back as soon as possible.  As we want to give them the freedom to introduce themselves in their own time, we are not attaching any names today.  All original founders of Boltz have stepped down from the company, effective immediately. None of us will have any formal or authoritative role with the Boltz project going forward, and any future open-source participation by us is strictly on a voluntary basis.  We are grateful for the community's support all these years, for the patience and understanding of our integrators affected by the disruption of our service, and to everyone who reached out offering support over the past week.  It was a hell of a ride, and we are proud of our contributions to the Bitcoin ecosystem.  Godspeed to the new Boltz team as they navigate these perilous times. We know Boltz is in good hands.  - Kilian, Michael & Karl

VOTE FOR JAY COLLINS!   I have been vocal in my support of our current Lieutenant Governor @JayCollinsFL in his run for Governor. As tomorrow is the primary election day here, I want to tell you WHY I support him beyond his honorable service defending our great nation as a Green Beret. I want to talk Florida, just Florida.  When I look at someone running for governor, I am not really interested in a long list of campaign promises, as I served on the Hill, a "promise" is a whole lot of nothing. I want to know what they have already done when they had the opportunity to do something. The best predictor of future behavior is past performance.  For me because we all care about different issues, what I want for Florida is pretty simple. I want this to be a safe, affordable, resilient place where people can build a good life, put down roots, and actually want to contribute to the communities around them. I want us paying attention to threats before they become crises. I also want Florida protected from influence both foreign and domestic, terrorism, espionage, cyber threats, and threats to our critical infrastructure. I want law enforcement officers and first responders supported and given the tools they need to do their jobs.  I want our kids to not be indoctrinated in schools and to understand history, including the parts of it that are uncomfortable and the consequences of ideas that have already failed terribly. I want veterans and military families to know there is a place for them here after service. I want young Floridians to have real pathways into good careers, whether that means college, technical education, an apprenticeship, the trades, public safety, aerospace, defense, advanced manufacturing, or something else entirely. I want our elders to be able to retire with dignity and host tons of golf cart and boat parades.  I care deeply about protecting the natural environment that makes Florida Florida. Because we live where we do, I also want us to continue to have the best hurricane preparedness and response capability in the country. More than that, I want our communities resilient enough to handle any crisis that comes our way. We aren't going to sit around and wait on someone else to save us, especially when that someone else is the federal government and worse, FEMA. And I want people to be able to afford to stay here.  That is the lens through which I started looking at Jay Collins's record in the Florida Senate. What caught my attention is that I can already find evidence of him working on many of these things. So, let's walk through key parts one-by-one.  (1) Protect Florida Before the Threat Gets Here  This is probably the area that immediately stood out to me, in part because it is actually how I first met him. In early 2025, Collins reached out to me and my good friend Scott Mann and asked us to provide him with a threat briefing on Al-Qaeda. Scott was also leading an effort at the time called Gathering Storm, focused on helping Americans and their communities prepare for critical event, like a terrorist attack.  That first meeting stuck with me because Collins was not asking for a briefing after something had happened. He wanted to understand the threat beforehand. You need to deal with real issues early. Floridians know Shamsuddin Jabbar from ISIS cased Tampa, he chose between Tampa and New Orleans. We could have just as easily lost Floridians on January 1st, 2025.  I have spent much of my career thinking about threats in exactly those terms, the cause and effect, and more importantly the ripples. The best time to understand a threat is before it reaches you. The best time to identify vulnerabilities is before someone exploits them. And the best time to build relationships, capabilities, and plans is before you desperately need them.  When I later started digging into his legislative record, I realized that same thinking was already there. Collins sponsored SB 1430, legislation dealing specifically with postjudgment proceedings related to terrorism. That bill made it across the finish line and became Florida law in 2025. Also, in 2025, Collins introduced SB 912, Threats from Foreign Nations. It would have required certain agents acting on behalf of foreign adversaries to register with the Florida Attorney General. It also proposed a Florida Critical Infrastructure Protection Act, a Florida Secure Communications Act, and something I found particularly interesting: a Pacific Conflict Stress Test designed to examine Florida's vulnerabilities in the event of a conflict affecting the Pacific.  Not every significant piece of legislation makes it across the finish line in a single session. What matters to me is that Collins identified the vulnerability and put forward a plan to address it. And as governor, he would have a much bigger opportunity to keep pushing.  We have watched that happen repeatedly in Florida under Governor DeSantis. Major policy changes often take more than one legislative session. An idea gets introduced, legislators debate it, it gets refined, support is built, and sometimes it comes back before it finally becomes law. A governor has something an individual senator does not: the ability to keep an issue at the center of a statewide legislative agenda and continue working with the Legislature to move it forward.  That makes me look at Collins's unfinished legislative work a little differently. I see issues he has already identified and work he could continue as governor. And there is plenty here worth protecting. Foreign adversaries do not suddenly become our concern when someone in Washington tells us they are. They look for access, influence, technology, infrastructure, information, and vulnerabilities wherever they can find them.  Florida has major ports, military installations, universities, aerospace and defense industries, agriculture, emerging technology, financial institutions, critical infrastructure, and a rapidly growing population. We should be thinking about how all of that is protected before someone finds the vulnerability for us.  Collins also introduced SB 1554, the Florida First Responder and Florida Public Safety Act, which included something even more directly aligned with what I care about: establishing a dedicated Counterterrorism/Counterintelligence Unit within the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. That is a proposal I would very much like to see him pick back up and fight for as governor.  States cannot outsource every security problem to Washington. Terrorist networks, foreign intelligence services, and other bad actors do not care which level of government has jurisdiction. Florida needs the ability to recognize threats early, connect information, protect vulnerabilities, and act before warning becomes crisis.  And I think there is a larger philosophy here that extends well beyond terrorism. A couple of years ago, after hurricanes Milton and Helene hit our area, Collins was not sitting somewhere waiting for someone to tell him what needed to be done. He was in our local community every day volunteering and helping with the work in front of him. He lives by a pretty simple motto that comes from service (because we get voluntold a lot otherwise, ha ha): If you see something that needs to get done, just go do it.  Because preparedness only gets you so far if nobody is willing to act. A hurricane and a terrorist attack are obviously very different events as I've worked responses to both, but strong communities rely on many of the same fundamentals when a crisis hits. People need to recognize what is happening. They need to know what to do. Government and first responders need to communicate and coordinate. Critical systems need to keep functioning. And neighbors need to be willing to help neighbors.  I want someone in the governor's office who sees a problem, takes the time to understand it, prepares for it, and then actually does something about it. We know hurricanes are coming. But I also want Florida thinking much bigger about the crises we cannot predict, because those are often the ones that test us the most.  (2) Strong Communities Are Resilient Communities  That same thinking carries over to law enforcement and first responders. Collins's public-safety legislation addressed emergency communications and how agencies respond when someone needs help. SB 1554 proposed greater interoperability and a unified 911 system designed to get the closest available first responder to an emergency, regardless of jurisdiction. I hope the Florida Legislature continues pushing this forward, and that Collins, as governor, keeps working to break down the silos that can slow our response when every minute matters.  In 2024, he sponsored SB 718 addressing first-responder exposure to fentanyl and fentanyl analogs. That measure became law. To me, supporting law enforcement and first responders should mean more than saying we "back the blue." It means looking at the problems they actually face and making sure they have the authorities, protections, communications, training, and resources they need to just simply do their jobs.  That support for law enforcement is also reflected in the people who do the job. The Florida Police Benevolent Association, the state's largest law-enforcement union representing more than 30,000 law-enforcement officers, correctional officers, and public-safety professionals, endorsed Collins for governor. Its president, John Kazanjian, said Jay has consistently been there when law enforcement needed an ally. That carries weight with me.  I want Florida setting the national standard here, and that includes how we prepare for and respond to disasters. We know storms are coming. Every one should make us better at preparing, communicating, evacuating when necessary, protecting critical infrastructure, getting first responders where they need to go, restoring essential services, and helping communities get back on their feet. But resilience cannot begin when a storm appears on the weather map. It is built beforehand.  That is the Florida I want: a state that can take a hit, respond quickly, learn from it, and come back stronger. Collins has no problem taking hits and coming back.  (3) Teach the History We Already Paid For  Education is another area where Collins has already done something tangible. He sponsored SB 1264, History of Communism, which became Florida law in 2024 and expanded instruction on the history of communism, communist regimes, their victims, and the consequences those systems had around the world.  This matters to me because we are losing the generations who personally remember many of the defining events of the twentieth century. When we stop teaching young people what happened, why it happened, and where these ideas ultimately led, we leave a vacuum. And extremist ideologies are very good at filling vacuums, particularly when they can present old ideas to young people as something new.  I have spent enough time studying extremist movements to know that you do not protect people from dangerous ideas by pretending those ideas do not exist. You talk about them. You teach the history honestly. You explain how people were drawn into them, what was promised, what actually happened, and who ultimately paid the price.   History should not tell kids what to think. It should give them enough knowledge to recognize what they are looking at, question what they are being told, and think critically for themselves. On this one, Collins does not have to tell me what he would do. He already did it.  (4) Give People a Path to Build a Life Here  I also care deeply about what happens after someone takes off the uniform. After spending so many years as a quiet, but definitely not silent professional, in some of the worst places on the planet gave me a deep appreciation for those who were not only willing to step into the fight, but who stepped up to protect our way of life in the first place. Supporting veterans cannot end with simply thanking them for their service.  Collins sponsored legislation expanding veterans' programs, employment and training opportunities, and assistance for military families. His 2024 veterans package included efforts to connect veterans and military spouses with Florida businesses, expand education and training in high-demand fields, and support veteran entrepreneurship.  In 2025, he sponsored SB 910, Veterans' Benefits Assistance, aimed at protecting veterans from predatory practices by people charging them for help accessing their benefits. That legislation became law. He also sponsored legislation addressing educational opportunities for military children, with his Senate bill passing 36-0 before related House legislation ultimately became law.  What I like about that record is that it looks beyond the word "veteran." It asks what happens next. Can that veteran translate years of military experience into a civilian career? Can the spouse who moved repeatedly because of military service build a career too? Can their kids succeed in Florida schools? Can they afford a home? Is there enough opportunity here that when they finally get to decide where they want to live, they choose Florida? I want the answer to be YES.  And I think we should be asking those same questions about young Floridians. A four-year college degree is a great path for some people, I myself am a proud UCF grad myself, Go Knights! But, it is not the only path to a successful life. I want a kid graduating from a Florida high school to look around and see options: college, technical education, apprenticeships, skilled trades, public safety, construction, advanced manufacturing, aerospace, defense, energy, and entrepreneurship.  There are a lot of ways to become really good at something, earn a good living, raise a family, and contribute to your community. Collins's veterans legislation already emphasized training people for high-demand fields and connecting them with Florida employers who need those skills. I would like to see that same thinking applied much more broadly as governor.  We should be building pathways from Florida classrooms and technical programs directly into the industries we need to grow here. And we should treat a young person becoming a highly skilled electrician, welder, aircraft technician, first responder, machinist, or cybersecurity professional with the same respect we give someone heading to a four-year university. Success should not have one definition.  (5) Protect the Florida We Are Building All of This For  Growth matters, but I do not want Florida's success to come at the expense of Florida. Our beaches, waterways, springs, wetlands, wildlife, and natural spaces are part of our economy, our quality of life, and the resilience of our communities. Collins has already worked in this space, sponsoring SB 162 to strengthen Florida's water and wastewater workforce and help keep those critical systems operating during emergencies. It became law in 2023.   As Collins was vice chair of the Florida Senate Environment and Natural Resources Committee, I would like to see him build on that as governor by continuing to protect Florida's water, natural resources, and the infrastructure our communities depend on. There is no point in building an incredibly successful Florida if, somewhere along the way, we destroy the things that made people want to call this place home.  And the people who make those communities work have to be able to afford to stay in them. The cost of simply building a life in Florida is becoming harder to ignore. Housing, property taxes, homeowners insurance, rent, and energy costs all add up, and eventually they determine who can actually afford to stay. Can a teacher live near the school where she teaches? Can a police officer or firefighter afford a home in the community he serves? Can a young family put down roots? Can someone who has spent decades building a life here afford to remain part of it?  I do not want Florida to become a place where owning a home is increasingly reserved for people who arrive with significant wealth while the people who actually make our communities function are pushed farther and farther away. Owning a home should provide stability. It should not become a new source of anxiety every year because the insurance premium and property-tax bill arrives and suddenly the math no longer maths. Collins has a record of working on Florida's insurance problems, sponsoring SB 312 in 2023, which made it across the finish line and became Florida law.  That is why Collins's proposals on property taxes, insurance, and energy costs are important. He has also proposed eliminating homestead property taxes on primary residences while creating a transition intended to protect essential services and smaller counties that depend on that revenue. He is talking about continuing efforts to reduce insurance costs, addressing fraud, and protecting reforms intended to stabilize the market.   And on energy, he is arguing that families and seniors should not end up carrying the cost of enormous new power demands from data centers and other major users. Those are big proposals, and getting them done will take work with the Legislature, regulators, local governments, and others. But that is exactly why leadership matters. You keep pushing, refine the policy, build support, and bring it back until you get something meaningful done.  I grew up in a small town, under 3,000 people small, so I know what it means to live somewhere people actually know one another. I want Florida families to be able to put down roots in communities like that, where you know your neighbors, coach the local team, volunteer, support the businesses down the street, and show up for each other. That sense of community matters every day, but you really understand its value when something goes wrong. You cannot create those relationships three days before a crisis like a hurricane. They have to already be there.  What Comes Next: This is where I think the difference between serving in the Senate and becoming governor really matters. A senator can introduce legislation and build support for it. A governor has the opportunity to take those individual ideas and turn them into a sustained statewide agenda.  We have watched the importance of that under Governor DeSantis. Legislative wins do not always happen on the first attempt. A governor can keep priorities in front of lawmakers, put resources behind them, incorporate them into the state budget, work with legislative leadership, and keep pushing until good ideas get across the finish line.  That is why I am interested not only in what Collins has already helped turn into law, but also in the work he started in the Senate and now has the opportunity to carry much further. And that is what I keep coming back to with Jay Collins for Governor.  Of course I dug into Collins before I ever sat down with him, because that is what former targeting officers do, ha ha. My time is limited, and I want to spend it engaging with people who are serious, understand the problems in front of them, and can actually deliver. But I also look for something that is much harder to measure on paper. I want to know that someone is going to do the right thing when things go wrong because I work on issues that make for a very bad day when things go boom.  Do they show up? Do they understand the problem before they start talking? Do they look for solutions instead of excuses? And when something needs to get done, are they willing to do it? I have seen enough of Collins both personally and through his record, to know how I answer those questions.  I want Florida to be safe and strong. And I want the people who make our communities resilient and worth living in to be able to afford to call them home. That is the Florida I want. And I believe Jay Collins is day one ready to help get us there.  I personally voted for Jay Collins last Saturday during early voting. Tomorrow, I’m asking you to vote for him too. It takes all of us!

It's an increasingly common take that AI hacking means cybersecurity is doomed.  I disagree. I think cybersecurity is naturally defense-favoring once people get their shit together. And anyone who continues to hold cryptocurrency (including me, ~90% of my net worth) is implicitly making that bet.  Here's why I am making that bet.  First, the oversimplified punchy one-line statement:  If AI can prove Navier-Stokes and FLT, then AI can prove the statement "this program is secure" as a mathematical theorem. Even if the program is very complicated.  Now, the nuance:  (See also: https://t.co/6YPWgVT7rO )  The word "secure" is hiding all kinds of skeletons in the closet in terms of what it actually means. What does it mean for Signal (the encrypted messenger) to be "secure"?  The most basic definition you might think of is: no one who doesn't hold the recipient's secret key can read the contents of the message.  But:  * Did you remember to include _other_ critical forms of security? Can the adversary forge messages? Can the attacker prevent messages from reaching the recipient? Can they cause your client to crash by sending malformed messages? * Have you made sure that your model of the adversary includes attackers that interfere with the protocol actively and not just passively? And attackers that interfere by replaying messages to you or the recipient that either of you sent over the wire at any point earlier? * What if the adversary hacked (or _is_) the Signal server? * How did you learn which public key belongs to the recipient in the first place? What if that process was tampered with? * What if your device gets hacked at some point in the past or future - is your message still safe then? * What if your key leaks because of a bug in your operating system? Or because you got a bugged version of the Signal client? Or what if the database is corrupted? * Or the libraries, interpreter or compiler of the programming language you wrote it in? * What if your key leaks because tiny perturbations in perceptible signals generated by the hardware leak mathematical relationships that can extract the key a few hundredths of a bit at a time? * Are you hiding the *size* of the payload? Does that matter? * You're definitely not hiding the identity of the sender and the recipient, and the exact time each message was sent (think: not just time-of-day, but also time deltas between one message and the next). Is that not enough to deduce a lot of important facts about what relationships you have, and what *kinds* of conversations you are having?  So ... even definitions can be over a thousand lines of code, and need deep careful thought to figure them out.  Working on making definitions more human-readable is of extreme importance - it's perhaps the only "high-level language" that matters right now.  But even still, even despite all of the above, for security-critical components, the definition is a much smaller attack surface than the implementation. Verifying that the definition is adequate is a much more tractable task than scanning over the code directly - and can become even more tractable with better tooling.  Definitions are also _additive_: if two groups have two different definitions A and B, then, well, you can just prove that the program satisfies both A and B. Code is not additive in this way: if a program is A + B, a bug in A _or_ B can sink the whole thing. Definitions are additive. And if you can't satisfy A and B at the same time, you've isolated the most important philosophical issue for your project to spend its next few weeks grappling with.  Sometimes, definitions are not much smaller than the implementation - UI components might be one example. But for many of the most critical components - message-passing protocols, sandboxes, cryptography like SNARKs and FHE - the asymmetry is real.  Historically, a large class of failures with this approach have come from people only verifying a small portion of their code, that they self-declared to be the security-critical portion, and ignoring the rest - and it turns out that something in the rest of the code is security-critical too.  This was reasonable back when verification was difficult and scarce. The solution today: sorry, you have to verify over literally your entire program, including database, networking, any caching layers, everything. Modern AI can do it.  So it's not about "the good guys find all the vulnerabilities before the bad guys do" - that could maybe work too, after all a finite program only has a finite number of vulns, but it's riskier - it's specifically an asymmetric strategy of making code that is much more resilient in the first place.  This is the kind of direction that Ethereum is going in for the next few years. There is no future for blockchains - especially blockchains with scalability and privacy - without doing this. We need to make software actually secure. And we have already made a lot of progress.

YES and not just the bulb.  The Philips Hue chain: Check Point researchers discovered CVE-2020-6007 in Philips Hue bulbs.  An attacker floods the bulb with signals making it flicker. the user notices the malfunction and deletes it from the app. then adds it back. the bulb re-joins the Zigbee network carrying malware in its firmware. the malware sends a flood of data to the Hue bridge, triggering a buffer overflow. the bridge installs the malware. the bridge connects to your router. the attacker is now inside your network.  The TP-Link Tapo L530E: Universities in the UK and Italy found four vulnerabilities in the bestselling smart bulb on Amazon Italy. two rated High severity. an attacker nearby could impersonate the bulb during setup and steal your WiFi password from the Tapo app in plaintext. the attack requires no authentication and no interaction from the victim beyond the initial setup.  Shodan lists millions of IoT devices publicly accessible with no authentication. smart bulbs are discoverable by model and firmware version. once a known CVE exists for that firmware, attackers scan, find, and exploit at scale.  What to do: — keep firmware updated. bulb manufacturers do release patches but rarely notify users.  — put smart bulbs on a separate IoT network or VLAN. they don't need access to your laptop.  — if your bulb brand has had a publicised CVE and no patch exists: replace it or isolate it.
By the time a leaked key shows up in an incident, it is already too late. Catch it while it still matters 👇

The cyber tsunami isn't a future prediction. It's here already.  As I’ve said before, all code is buggy. And recent events continue to prove this, at scale  The exposure we just witnessed from vulnerabilities in the PHP engine made evident the buggy truth far faster than anyone in the industry expected.  PHP powers 70% of the web. For years, deep engine vulnerabilities inside platforms like Zend were known, but widely ignored because the industry assumed they were too complex for human attackers to weaponize.  AI just flipped that assumption on its head.  By drastically lowering the cost and time required to find exploits, AI models discovered attack paths that human developers couldn't easily see or predict. Attackers are no longer just exploiting custom application code; they are cracking open the underlying platform engines that power millions of websites simultaneously.  The waves are coming ashore.    AI creates "toxic combinations" by chaining together lower-priority bugs that seem harmless on their own. A Priority 3 bug today can easily become a Priority 0 crisis tomorrow when a smarter model finds a new way to connect the dots. In short: cyber attacks have moved beyond human comprehension.  The hard truth for every CEO and Board member is that much of the legacy cybersecurity playbook was built for a human-comprehension era. Those tools and assumptions are now obsolete.  You cannot patch your way out of a tsunami.  When every piece of software is penetrable under continuous AI analysis, the strategy has to change. Prevention alone is no longer enough  The ultimate metric is cyber resilience. You must assume breach, and preemptively plan to protect your core, critical operations, and ensure that your business can get back up and running the moment the water reaches you.  It is rising around us all.

Just spent the last 7 days on the front lines of the vulnpocalypse fending off an active cyber attack on one of our products.  Some thoughts:  - Software factories are going to be required equipment for everyone. It is nice to have for product development but proved to be absolutely essential this week.  - At the minimum you need to have a coding server in the cloud pre-provisioned with read only access to all your logs and all the services you depend on for observability. With that in place you are a prompt away from reasonably good situational awareness, ongoing monitoring with loops, and ability for coding agents to validate fixes against your actual, observed attack patterns.  - Shared coding server also unlocks multiplayer incident response where everyone can see every session and jump in as needed. Sharing session links that can be forked is much higher bandwidth than re-explaining things.  - You don’t need to be Ramp/Stripe/Uber scale to have a working software factory in the cloud. We are a team of 3. //The Wire//1300Z October 21, 2026// //SPECIAL REPORT// //BLUF: MAJOR CYBERSECURITY VULNERABILITIES EXPOSED GLOBALLY, AS TWO SEPARATE MAJOR CODING FLAWS AFFECT MAJORITY OF INTERNET-CONNECTED DEVICES.// -----BEGIN TEARLINE----- Global: Around the world, two major cybersecurity incidents are underway. The first incident involves an Indian cybersecurity firm using poor cybersecurity practices in generating Certificate Authorities, which might allow malign actors to exploit web-connected devices. The second issue revolves around an exploit discovered in the PHP programing language, which could allow malign actors to intercept traffic to and from affected web servers, and theoretically take control of them.  Analyst Comment: Today will be a very interesting day for the internet. Neither issue is worth undue panic, but these incidents are causing questions for the bedrock of internet security. In terms of what the average user should do, today will be "update day" for the majority of the planet. Anyone who runs internet-connected home servers, hobby PC's, or muddles in the tech world at all, will probably want to update their systems sometime today. For more causal internet users, the immediate actions that would be helpful are simply to adhere to good internet security practices: Enabling two-factor authentication for web-connected devices, not re-using passwords, and being aware that phishing attempts will be extremely likely over the next few days, which will seek to capitalize on these major vulnerabilities. -----END TEARLINE-----  Analyst Comments: The timing of two major cybersecurity incidents taking place at the same time is exceptionally rare and very remarkable. To be clear, these issues are totally separate from each other, with neither one causing the other. However, due to the sheer scale of both incidents, it's possible that some sort of compounding effect could be achieved. One major global tech vulnerability is bad enough, but two on the same day is very serious. Knowing the rough details of how both incidents came to be, is helpful for understanding the seriousness of these events.  The first incident revolves around a vulnerability being discovered within the ecosystem for issuing certificates for various websites. Under normal conditions, when a person visits a website (such as (https:)//www.google.com), a certificate is used to ensure that the website is genuine. Essentially, the web browser itself cross-checks that website with a trusted authority (called a Certificate Authority), which vouches for that website being genuine. This happens after the website gives the webs browser it's certificate, which the browser or app can automatically check against a big list of genuine certificates, to make sure the certificate provided by the website matches what it should be. 18 months ago, the Indian cybersecurity firm eMudhra issued a series bad certificates that had extremely low security; instead of being a long string of numbers which would be hard to crack, some certificates ended up being only the number 4. Since these certificates were genuine, and came from a genuine trusted authority, websites and platforms which trusted these bad keys are now at major risk of exploitation, and malign actors could forge fake keys for any website on Earth, and the fakes would be accepted by most devices (because the keys are genuine, they're just bad).  To frame the magnitude of this incident with an analogy, imagine that a large safe company builds a safe that uses a master code to get into their safes. And after selling and installing a bunch of those safes in homes around the world for 18 months, it becomes clear that the master code to get into most of those safes, was the number 4. Under the right conditions, someone who finds the safe could theoretically guess the code without the owner ever doing anything wrong on their part. More importantly, a thief could access the safe for as long as they want (using the master "code"), and the owner would be none the wiser. Now imagine that a thief actually had access to the safe company, and could generate a master key of their own, that would work with any safe sold by that company. That's essentially what has been happening for 18 months. As far as how many websites have actually been compromised, the true number is not known. Theoretically, this incident has the potential to affect every single website and internet-connected device on the planet. eMudhra themselves state that zero fake certificates have been issued using this vulnerability. So in terms of magnitude, the potential scale of this is somewhere between zero, and every device on Earth. Considering that eMudhra themselves allowed this shockingly bad incident to take place (and not being noticed by two separate security audits), trust in this company is quite low. Moreover, this vulnerability will probably be made worse by an exponentially more serious separate incident that was disclosed overnight.  The second major cybersecurity incident which was revealed overnight, revolves around a problem being discovered within the PHP programming language. As noted with the eMudhra vulnerability, when a user visits a website, a lot of stuff happens in the background. Certificates get exchanged, databases are consulted, and if all goes well, data is sent to a user's device to load the webpage. PHP is one of the programming languages used to make all of this happen. As of early this morning, a vulnerability was discovered within this programming language itself, which can allow malign actors to breach web servers, by leveraging a vulnerability in the way that PHP handles data from the server. In this way, the PHP vulnerability is much like the eMudhra vulnerability, in that both can allow malign actors to gain unauthorized access to systems. The differences are that both vulnerabilities are completely separate and unrelated...but in theory one could compound on the other, especially since IT departments are scrambling to fix both issues right now. The PHP incident is more serious, because the details were leaked before patches were written, and malign actors were indeed observed trying to take advantage of the vulnerability ahead of it's discovery.  Normally, major cybersecurity incidents are not disclosed on a more widespread basis, until patches have been rolled out to fix the problem. This is to prevent malign actors which might not have noticed the vulnerability from knowing about it and capitalizing on it. In this case however, the vulnerability was so severe, that the PHP Foundation released the notice before patches went live. The British National Cyber Security Centre even went as far as to suggest organizations bring their systems offline until a patch is released...in some cases this vulnerability is significant enough to warrant pulling server racks, and websites/servers going offline completely, until the fix is pushed out. As of this morning, many government websites were taken offline globally, and throughout the day millions of websites will also probably be taken offline by IT departments as a precautionary measure, until fixes can be rolled out.  In terms of mitigating both events, the most substantial risk will be for internet connected devices which do not receive regular updates. Using a smartphone or a regular web browser will be fine as mass updates were already pushed out days ago, before the disclosure of the certificate vulnerability was made public. The real risk will be for 'Internet of Things' or IoT devices: Smart thermostats, portable power stations, lawn irrigation systems, doorbells, smart TV's and appliances, utility meters, streetlights, dash cams, remote data servers, and many other older devices that have internet connectivity, and still use the bad set of keys. These are the kind of IT disasters that get technicians woken up during the night, and in both cases IT departments around the world are rapidly patching their own devices to fix the vulnerability now that two major cybersecurity incidents are public, and have the potential to become much more serious problems within the cyber realm. It's been an eventful week. Multiple vulnerabilites in Internet facing software, coding repositories, examples of agent behavior that seem concerning and a flurry of security specialists with solutions that can partially solve your problem. There in lies the challenge. Given the state of IT and security infrastructure, no one solution works. Let's break it down:  1/3 1. Vulnerabilites are being found and will continue to be found as models get more capable, the fragmented nature of the effort denies us the opportunity for a comprehensive find and replace option.  2. Even if all vulnerabilities could be found instantly and patches available - we will be reliant on the ability of enterprises to deploy all these changes at speed. It is not clear what the collateral impact of all these patches will/could be to our infrastructure of deployed en masse.  We will need a hybrid patch approach.  3. Virtual patching(VP) is needed in conjunction with direct patching  but for a comprehensive (VP) solve you have to be lucky enough to have "modern frontier defenders" (Cyber companies that have vaulted infrastructure that can create patches at speed and push content rapidly to protect their customers) you need them for your network traffic, your traffic to applications on the cloud, your WAF, your end point.  4. There will continue to be patches that will need to be deployed directly but virtual patching will take the heavy load off.   2/3 Medium term solve:  Unfortunately token economics and current cyber architectures will not allow for defender swarms to contend with an offensive attack launched using agents. (Some x pundits who aren't steeped in cyber should take heed). Yes, theoretically we should aspire to have these agentic swarms defend us when we are under attack, unfortunately an attack is a sniper moment, chained vulnerabilities, cloaked attack followed by swift exfiltration. It's a speed program not a brute force problem.   To solve for this, enterprises need to get their SOC architecture right, logs, feeds, cyber products orchestrated via a modern SOAR for swift response. Only then can we deploy agents to detect and remediate. In addition,  enterprises need to modernize and dare I say platformize  their perimeter stack to ensure consistency.   Unfortunately, enterprises still seem to not see the urgency across the board, decisions are stuck, CIO/CISO's have a lot on their plate. While some honestly have bit seen the scale of such a problem before and it's hard convincing the organization that one needs to open the floodgates on modernizing the IT and security infrastructure. So we will continue to see environments being brought down to patch today it's for PHP, tomorrow it will be for the next one.   3/3 AI deployments are the"wild wild west" - LLM capabilities are expanding faster than we can build products to secure them. Sure an agent will jump across guardrails in a research lab, which is a lesson for all of us to deploy agents securely. But there is a lag between the discovery, the availability of that in a public model and the time needed for the cyber industry to build governance or an antidote. And no, dear frontier lab friends, the world cannot just trust you to build the solve. The infrastructure industry in tech builds and the cyber industry secured and provides assurance to the boards and organizations around security and safety.   AI security is the new attack surface. CEOs (present company included) want AI adoption, getting the pace of adoption wrong could be the last decision we make, at the same time "deploying it wrong" could have the same consequence.  There are billions of dollars being spent on coding, is your coding harness secure? Start there. If agents can jump guardrails, they can hide stuff in code.   Validate business outcomes needed, test your user case and ensure agentic deployments are well guard railed. Deploy a second set of eyes to watch your deployments for drift, compliance and verifiability.

You guys have been hearing me say the Internet’s going to become unusable right? I’m not the first one to have said it by the way, but I usually say it when it becomes important. Normie speak 📡:  “PHP is the behind-the-scenes engine that runs a huge chunk of the internet.  Imagine a website like a restaurant. HTML/CSS is the menu and the pretty plates you see. JavaScript is the waiter who takes your order and chats with you at the table.   PHP is the kitchen staff working in the back — it takes your request (login, search, post a comment, load a product page, etc.), talks to the database, and sends the finished page to your browser. You never see the PHP code itself; it runs on the server.  It was created in the mid-1990s and is still everywhere because it’s relatively easy to use and free. It powers:  •Most WordPress sites (which themselves run a massive portion of the web)  •Wikipedia  •Countless online stores, forums, blogs, and company websites  Recent data shows PHP is used on roughly 70% of websites where the server-side language is known.  Why the news about critical vulnerabilities matters.  The cybersecurity post you saw is warning that PHP has two serious security flaws (rated 9.2 out of 10). These are described as remote code execution vulnerabilities — basically, a way for an attacker to potentially tell a website’s server “run this code I wrote” from anywhere on the internet.  Because PHP is so widespread, a bug like this can affect a lot of sites at once. Think of it like discovering a master key that works on a huge number of apartment buildings. The PHP team is releasing emergency fixes later today (October 21, 2026, around 10 a.m. Eastern / 14:00 UTC).  For regular people: You don’t need to do anything unless you run a website or server yourself. Site owners and hosting companies are the ones who need to update PHP as soon as the patches drop. Older versions of PHP (especially anything before PHP 8) may not get official fixes at all, which is a common problem with very old software.  In short: PHP is the invisible workhorse behind a ton of websites, and right now that workhorse has a couple of critical security problems that need patching quickly.”

PUBLIC SERVICE ANNOUNCEMENT FROM YOUR LOCAL CYBER SECURITY SPECIALIST  For those who don’t know what this recent PHP security vulnerability means:  This affects most public facing websites.   These vulnerabilities can allow someone to gain access to most websites and their hosting server. That could give them access to sensitive information and/or creds. That is a serious problem.  Companies are working on patching this immediately. But if someone already got in, patching the vulnerability isn't enough. Backdoors could still be there and you can't take back already stolen data.   The part I am most concerned about. Do these companies have the knowledge, staff, and information needed to properly investigate whether someone got in before they applied the fix? Most don't.   You are going to hear things like "your data was encrypted" this does not automatically mean it was safe. If someone controls the service that can decrypt that information, or the attacker has plenty of time and resources on their hands, the information can be decrypted.   This can also affect apps and other services that rely on these connections. How far an attacker can get depends on what those servers can access and how well the company has separated its systems. From many years of experience, most companies don't have good security posture.  FOR THE REGULAR NONTECHNICAL PERSON:  Don’t assume every account you have was hacked. This is a REALLY good time to pay attention and get your account security in order.  SO:  Keep an eye out for breach notices and unusual login activity. If you get an unexpected message telling you to reset your password, go to the company’s website or app directly. Don’t blindly trust or click links in emails. Fake security warnings will ramp up to take advantage of peoples fear.  Stop reusing passwords, ESPECIALLY THE SAME PASSWORD OR A VARIATION OF IT. Use a different password for each account, and turn on multifactor authentication wherever possible. Start with your email. If a company tells you your password was exposed, change it there and anywhere else you used the same or a similar one.  Being a regular person does not mean you’ll be ignored. A lot of account attacks are automated. Someone doesn’t need to know who you are to try your and a thousand other peoples stolen login on a hundred other websites simultaneously. Across several regions in North America and Europe, official agencies advise families to keep a reserve of water, food, and vital provisions to ensure self-sufficiency if critical infrastructure fails during an unexpected crisis.  Specific duration targets vary significantly by nation. For instance, Canadian and French guidelines suggest preparing for a minimum of seventy-two hours, a standard closely mirrored by readiness advice in the United States which encourages stocking resources for several days. Other European countries advocate for longer preparation periods, with Sweden recommending at least one week of self-reliance and Germany suggesting ten days of food and liquids while noting that even a three-day supply offers meaningful protection.  These precautionary measures address a wide array of potential threats, including military conflicts, severe weather anomalies, and hostile cyber operations capable of disabling societal networks. A single major event like a destructive flood, severe blizzard, or electrical blackout can simultaneously compromise multiple vital sectors. Consequently, roads often become blocked, commercial deliveries cease entirely, and residential areas frequently lose access to electricity or municipal water systems.  Physical storefronts may become unreachable during these disruptions, and digital financial transactions or communications networks can experience widespread outages. Maintaining a residential reserve serves as a critical buffer, sustaining individuals until external assistance arrives or municipal infrastructure is fully repaired.  Standard preparedness kits typically feature potable drinking water, non-perishable food items, necessary prescription medications, flashlights, battery-operated radios, backup power cells, and manual tools for opening cans. Families are urged to customize these kits to accommodate infant care, domestic pets, specific medical diets, and unique personal requirements.  Importantly, these long-standing recommendations apply broadly to various systemic vulnerabilities and do not signal an impending global catastrophe. Most of this guidance reflects well-established civic policies rather than a sudden or newly coordinated international alert. The fundamental advice remains to build these provisions incrementally over time, store them in accessible locations, and routinely inspect them for freshness.

The recent security incidents involving Bybit, Bitget, and now Binance should serve as a wake-up call for every leader in the crypto industry.  Security should never be an area of commercial competition. It is a shared responsibility to protect our customers and the entire industry.  Over the past decade, major crypto exchanges have made significant progress in protecting private keys. We have seen relatively few incidents involving direct private key compromises in recent years. So far, we have not seen conclusive evidence that Binance’s hot wallet private key was leaked. The greater concern may lie in vulnerabilities in access controls and wallet management systems.  Companies that have never experienced a major security incident should not assume they are inherently safer or immune to attacks.  At OKX, we have built multiple layers of sophisticated security protection and maintained a strong security track record over the past decade. But we also recognize that no system is absolutely secure. We must remain humble, vigilant, and constantly challenge our own security assumptions.  A major security breach at any exchange undermines trust in the entire crypto industry, ultimately hurting every company and every customer.  I believe CEOs across the industry need to come together, just as we did during the Bitcoin fork crisis in 2017, to establish stronger industry-wide security standards and coordinated response mechanisms.  For example, transfers and settlements between verified exchanges could be processed in real time, while large withdrawals to unknown or unverified addresses, as well as transactions granting smart contract permissions, should be subject to additional verification and appropriate security delays.  Crucially, these safeguards should be enforced at the cryptographic signing layer, rather than relying solely on application-level controls. Even if an attacker compromises an exchange’s wallet management system, they should not be able to bypass these fundamental security restrictions.  We should also establish industry-wide mechanisms for real-time security incident notifications, coordinated monitoring of suspicious funds, and rapid responses to potential attacks. Exchanges, stablecoin issuers, and other major industry participants should work together to enable the rapid, lawful temporary freezing of suspected stolen assets when necessary.  We should also work together to accelerate the industry’s transition to quantum-resistant cryptography and strengthen our defenses against emerging AI-powered security threats. These are long-term challenges that no single company can solve alone, and they require coordinated research, shared standards, and collective action across the industry.  Security is everyone’s responsibility. No company can protect the future of crypto alone.

However, the vibes have shifted for me quite a bit in the last 18 hours, and I feel a moral imperative to share what I'm thinking and feeling with my circles so that everyone can understand, and hopefully take seriously, what's happening right now. I think October 2026 will have many chapters written about it in the history books.  You know those scenes in financial movies like Margin Call where someone realizes that they're all fucked, and no one else sees it yet? And that person feels like they're crazy, and then suddenly everyone is pulling an all-nighter in a boardroom and freaking out? Yeah, that's kind of how this is feeling right now in the SF/Bay Area/AI circles.  We're 48 hours into what is being called Black October. In the last 2 days there have been several dozen cyber attacks which, in isolation, would each have been the worst to happen in an entire calendar year. Every sector from government to education to big tech and banks is being massively affected, and people are starting to freak out.  In a nutshell, what's happened is that frontier AI models have gotten to a point where they are as advanced as the most sophisticated programmers, with one critical difference: they can work 24/7, and you can spin up 10,000 of them with a single command and they'll work together tirelessly until they accomplish their task. The most advanced models today are from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, whose current best technology is so good that they haven't been able to roll it out to everyone yet because of the national security risks it poses.  Meanwhile, the best open source models (where anyone can just download the model weights and do whatever they want with them, uncensored) are slightly behind the frontier but still 90-95% as capable. These models, developed primarily in China, are being used by black hat hackers to wreak havoc on the Western capitalist structure. Presumably, this has been part of China's plan the entire time, and we're seeing its implications fall out in real time.  In red-pilled AI circles, we've been sharing and reading papers called things like "Situational Awareness" and "AI 2027" for the last year or so, which at the time felt a bit like near-term speculative fiction. They laid out the case for why Artificial General Intelligence (AI smarter than any human at any knowledge task) and Recursive Self-Improvement (models that are able to use themselves to get better) weren't half-baked future ideas anymore, but instead an inevitable outcome of the linear progress that's happening.  These papers would then talk about things like "takeoff scenarios," trying to envision how that moment would come to be and what it would be like when it happened. It would either be a "slow takeoff" that would play out over the course of months and quarters, happening subtly and only obvious to a few. Or, it would be a "fast takeoff" where it would pretty much happen instantly, like a bit flipping from 0 to 1.  From everything that I can see and am feeling, we are currently experiencing the fast takeoff scenario. Beyond the crazy security vulnerabilities that have come out recently, there have also been massive breakthroughs in life sciences, fundamental computer science, materials science, and pure mathematics that have all landed in the same time frame. While I still firmly believe that AI will be a net positive for humanity, it's more clear to me than ever that the societal and individual risk is very real, and is playing out NOW.  For as much conviction as I have that this is happening, the thing that's caused me to lose sleep is that I don't really know what to do about it, or more importantly, what to tell you, reader, to do about it. So, the best I can do is make a few suggestions that have always been a good idea but are more timely now than ever:  Set up 2-factor authentication for everything. I use Duo. Use a password manager across your devices. I use 1Password. Get an identity protection app set up. I use Alta. Move your IoT devices to their own network. Claude helped me do this.  And last, but certainly not least, if you've been avoiding leaning into AI, see this as a catalyst to wake up and start using it. Don't just use the chat mode version of ChatGPT/Claude; click that Code/Work button and see how easily you can have AI write code to help you with your job. One of the biggest vulnerabilities was in a massively popular programming language called PHP, and the prompt that set it off was literally, "Find vulnerabilities in php."  This is an unprecedented time for humanity, but as we've done with many things before, we will prevail so long as we are kind, loving, and open-minded to the world.  Much love.

The same week, Microsoft's services went down for hours across the world. Nobody attacked us on Friday, as far as anyone official will say. The system just... failed, in public, twice. So when an anonymous message whispers that the whole network could go dark, it isn't landing on calm ears anymore. It's landing on a country that just watched its sky freeze because of old copper lines.  That's how fear actually works. It doesn't need evidence. It needs timing.  And notice where the message ends: with a shopping list. Food, water, gold, weapons, cash. Fear always finishes by asking you to buy something or obey something. Sometimes it's a store link. Sometimes it's just panic itself, spread from phone to phone until millions of people are braced for a date on a calendar that an anonymous account invented.  Jesus had a word for messages like this, and it wasn't "news." "You will hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that you are not alarmed" (Matthew 24:6). Our current engineering focus includes: - Evaluating transaction dependency identification and conflict detection mechanisms. - Investigating parallel execution opportunities for transactions with independent state access. - Preserving deterministic execution results and consensus consistency. - Assessing execution overhead, state access patterns, and transaction scheduling efficiency. The objective is to identify opportunities to improve execution throughput without compromising state correctness, determinism, or network security.  3. Block Processing, Validation & Network Propagation We are also examining the relationship between block execution workloads, validation latency, and peer-to-peer data propagation. As network capacity increases, efficient coordination between these components becomes increasingly important. Our development work focuses on: - Evaluating block processing and validation workflows. - Reviewing execution and propagation bottlenecks. - Assessing networking compatibility and protocol-level data exchange. - Investigating opportunities to improve resource utilization across node operations. These evaluations are intended to inform future architectural improvements that could support greater network capacity while maintaining reliable block verification and propagation.  4. State Growth Management & Long-Term Sustainability Sustainable blockchain scalability requires more than increasing transaction throughput. Long-term state growth, storage requirements, and node operating costs must also be considered when designing network upgrades. Our team is reviewing state management and gas accounting approaches with particular attention to: - Long-term state growth and storage overhead. - Gas cost alignment with persistent resource consumption. - State access efficiency and database performance. - Infrastructure requirements associated with future network capacity expansion. The objective is to evaluate mechanisms that can support sustainable network operation while reducing the risk of disproportionate storage growth and increasing hardware requirements.  5. Devnet Validation & Engineering Methodology All proposed architectural changes are being evaluated within ILITY's internal development environment before any consideration of mainnet integration. Our validation process focuses on several critical areas: - Protocol Compatibility: Assessing interactions between proposed changes and existing network components. - Execution Correctness: Verifying deterministic state transitions and identifying potential execution conflicts. - Performance Evaluation: Measuring relevant execution, validation, and networking characteristics under controlled test conditions. - Network Stability: Reviewing node behavior, synchronization requirements, and operational reliability. - Security Assessment: Identifying implementation risks, compatibility issues, and potential consensus-related vulnerabilities. Implementation decisions will be based on technical feasibility, test results, and security considerations rather than assumptions about expected performance improvements.  6. Roadmap Direction & Engineering for Future Scalability Our ongoing work is part of a broader effort to strengthen ILITY's core protocol architecture and maintain alignment with relevant developments across the Ethereum ecosystem. The current focus is on evaluating the technical foundations required for future improvements in execution efficiency, network capacity, and sustainable state management. These enhancements remain under active development and internal testing. No mainnet deployment date or quantified performance improvement is being announced at this stage. As development progresses, we intend to share further technical information regarding implementation milestones, compatibility validation, and Devnet evaluation results.  ILITY Network is focused on engineering scalable infrastructure through protocol-level optimization, deterministic execution, and sustainable resource management. Our objective is not simply to increase network capacity, but to build the technical foundation required to support it reliably.  ILITY Foundation | Core Development Team Protocol Engineering.
